hints: Think about what happens to the H atom that is replaced from the benzene ring when Br takes its place.
walkthrough:
See this as substitution, not addition**
Benzene keeps its aromatic ring in this reaction. One H on the ring is swapped for one Br, so the equation is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Br} + \text{other product}$. Count atoms to find what must combine with the displaced H.

hints: Remember benzene acts as a nucleophile here, its pi electrons attack the positive electrophile $\text{Br}^{+}$.
Think about what the ring looks like just after Br attaches but before $\text{H}^{+}$ leaves, the aromaticity is temporarily lost and positive charge is delocalised.
walkthrough:
Let the ring attack the electrophile**
Picture the delocalised pi cloud of benzene as electron rich. Draw a curly arrow starting in the middle of the ring (the pi system) and pointing to $\text{Br}^{+}$. That forms the new $\text{C-Br}$ bond.

Draw the temporary intermediate correctly**
Once Br bonds, that carbon becomes tetrahedral, it holds both Br and its original H. The aromatic circle is gone. Draw a cyclohexadienyl cation with a + charge delocalised over the remaining five carbons, often shown with two double bonds and a + in the ring. This is the Wheland intermediate.

Restore aromaticity by losing $\text{H}^{+}$**
Draw a second curly arrow starting from the $\text{C-H}$ bond on the same carbon as Br and pointing back into the ring. That electron pair reforms the pi system and ejects $\text{H}^{+}$, giving $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Br}$.

Final answer: Curly arrow from benzene pi system to $\text{Br}^{+}$ to form C-Br bond; intermediate is cyclohexadienyl cation with Br and H on same $sp^{3}$ carbon and positive charge delocalised around ring. Then curly arrow from C-H bond back into ring to reform aromatic pi system, releasing $\text{H}^{+}$.

hints: Focus on two facts, the attacking species $\text{Br}^{+}$ is electron loving, and an H is substituted by Br with the ring preserved.
walkthrough:
Name from what attacks and what happens**
$\text{Br}^{+}$ is an electrophile and it substitutes for H without destroying the benzene ring. Putting those two ideas together gives electrophilic substitution.

hints: Look at the change, benzene gains a $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ group, so this is alkylation of the ring.
Recall which type of reagent supplies an ethyl electrophile and which Lewis acid catalyst generates it.
walkthrough:
Recognise Friedel-Crafts alkylation**
Benzene to $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ is ethylbenzene formation. You need to attach an ethyl group by electrophilic substitution, the classic Friedel-Crafts alkylation.

Choose reagent and catalyst pair**
Use a haloethane such as $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$ as the source of $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}^{+}$. Use a strong Lewis acid such as anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_{3}$ to polarise the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond and generate the electrophile.

Final answer: reagent: chloroethane, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$ (or bromoethane / iodoethane)
catalyst: anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_{3}$ (or $\text{FeCl}_{3}$, $\text{FeBr}_{3}$)

hints: Remember hot alkaline $\text{KMnO}_{4}$ oxidises the whole alkyl side chain on benzene right back to the ring carbon, no matter how long it was.
walkthrough:
Apply the side chain oxidation rule**
Hot $\text{KMnO}_{4}$ with $\text{OH}^{-}(aq)$ is very vigorous. Any alkyl group directly on benzene is oxidised completely to a carboxylic group attached to the ring. So $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ becomes $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOH}$, which exists as $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COO}^{-}$ in alkali. Draw benzene with a $\text{COOH}$ (or $\text{COO}^{-}$) substituent.
Final answer: $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOH}$ (benzene ring with $\text{COOH}$ substituent, allowed as $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COO}^{-}$ / $\text{COONa}$ under alkaline conditions)

hints: In step 3, A with a $\text{COOH}$ group becomes $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, think which strong hydride reduces acids to primary alcohols but leaves the benzene ring alone.
In step 4, the benzene ring becomes a cyclohexane ring while $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ is unchanged, think which reagent adds hydrogen across pi bonds in rings.
walkthrough:
Reduce the acid to a primary alcohol**
Step 3 is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$. That is reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol. $\text{NaBH}_{4}$ is not strong enough, you need $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ in dry ether followed by acid work up.

Hydrogenate the ring only**
Step 4 is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{11}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$. The aromatic ring is fully hydrogenated to cyclohexane while the alcohol stays intact. Use hydrogen gas with a platinum catalyst, $\text{H}_{2}$ / Pt, with heat and pressure.

Final answer: step 3: $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$
step 4: $\text{H}_{2}$ with Pt catalyst (or Pt / $\text{H}_{2}$)

hints: Sketch $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{11}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ and label the ring carbons by their distance from the $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ attachment point to spot pairs that are mirror images.
walkthrough:
Count unique carbon environments**
Call the ring carbon attached to $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ C1. Moving round the ring, C2 and C6 are equivalent by symmetry, and C3 and C5 are equivalent, while C4 opposite the substituent is unique. That gives 4 different ring signals plus 1 signal for the exocyclic $\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ carbon, total $4 + 1 = 5$ peaks.
